Weight the objective by milestone year and by region

Source: R/objective-weights.R
setObjectiveWeights.Rd

Sets how much each (region, year) cell of total system cost counts in the objective. Two halves, declared separately and multiplied: years writes horizon@intervals$weight, regions writes config@objweight, and interpolation combines them into pObjWeight[region, year].

Usage

setObjectiveWeights(obj, ...)

# S4 method for class 'config'
setObjectiveWeights(obj, years = NULL, regions = NULL, reset = FALSE, ...)

# S4 method for class 'model'
setObjectiveWeights(obj, years = NULL, regions = NULL, reset = FALSE, ...)

# S4 method for class 'scenario'
setObjectiveWeights(obj, years = NULL, regions = NULL, reset = FALSE, ...)

Arguments

obj

a model, config or scenario.

...

unused, for method consistency.

years

the year half: a named numeric over milestone years (c("2035" = 0.5, "2045" = 0.5)), an unnamed numeric of one weight per milestone, or NULL to leave it alone. NA or 1 means the milestone counts in full.

regions

the region half: a named numeric over regions (c(R1 = 1, R2 = 0.6)), a data.frame(region, year, weight) for weights that differ by year as well, or NULL to leave it alone.

reset

logical; TRUE clears the half (or halves) named by a NULL argument instead of leaving it alone. setObjectiveWeights(mod, reset = TRUE) removes every weight.

Value

the object, with the weights written.

Details

The usual reason to weight a year is uneven time resolution. A milestone solved on a SAMPLE of the model calendar still carries full-year cost at full period weight – sample_calendar() annualises every sample – so a cheaply resolved interim year counts in the objective exactly as much as a fully resolved one, and several of them can dominate the sum. A weight below 1 says the estimate deserves less trust.

The usual reason to weight a region is that the study does not value every region's costs equally: differences in income level or purchasing power, a region modelled only as context, or a priority stated deliberately.

The weight scales the WHOLE cost cell – capital, fuel, variable cost, levies, penalties. That is what makes it safe: when every cost term in a cell scales by one factor, no trade-off inside the cell changes, so the cell's dispatch is what it would have been unweighted and only its share of the cross-cell investment decision moves. Weighting operating cost alone would shift the merit order inside the down-weighted cell toward fuel-burning plant. What the weight does change is capital: a down-weighted year's capital is charged less, which nudges investment earlier.

Weights are not interpolated. A cell no declaration names counts in full.

After a solve, objective_weights() reports the weighted objective beside the same sum recomputed without the weights, so the two can be compared without solving twice.

See also

objective_weights() to read them back after a solve, sample_calendar() and setCalendar() for the uneven-resolution case the year half exists for.

Examples

mod <- newModel("w", horizon = newHorizon(2030:2049, intervals = 5),
                region = c("R1", "R2"))
mid <- getHorizon(mod)@intervals$mid
# the interim milestones are solved on a sample, so trust them half
w <- stats::setNames(rep(0.5, length(mid) - 2L), mid[-c(1, length(mid))])
mod <- setObjectiveWeights(mod, years = w)
#> Error: `years` is unnamed, so it must give one weight per milestone (2) or a single weight for all; got 0.
#>   Name it by year instead to weight some milestones only.
getHorizon(mod)@intervals[, c("mid", "weight")]
#> Error in `[.data.table`(getHorizon(mod)@intervals, , c("mid", "weight")): column not found: [weight]
# and R2's costs count for 60%
mod <- setObjectiveWeights(mod, regions = c(R2 = 0.6))
mod@config@objweight
#>   region year weight
#> 1     R2   NA    0.6
